newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma slams Russian call to seize port.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma slams Russian call to seize port.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Saturday accused Russian politicians who have recently laid claim to Sevastopol, base of the Black Sea Fleet, of seeking conflict and said differences should be solved through dialogue.
"Unfortunately our relations are instilled with a cold spirit of alienation and mistrust from time to time," Kuchma said in a radio address.
"Not everyone in Russia has learned to accept Ukraine as a sovereign state yet," he added.
"It seems they are still confusing the present with the past, when everything that was said in Moscow resounded like thunder in every corner of the (Soviet) Union."

Kuchma mentioned no names but his comments were clearly directed at the Russian parliament which has passed resolutions aimed at halting the division of the former Soviet Black Sea Fleet between the two countries.

Earlier this month the Federation Council (upper house), following the State Duma (lower house), passed a resolution laying claim to Sevastopol as a Russian city and saying Ukraine had no right to govern it.

The resolution's sponsor, Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov, seen as a future presidential candidate, said on television this month the fleet's main base at Sevastopol, in the mostly Russia-speaking Crimean peninsula, could be reclaimed by force.

Diplomatic sources say Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko has written to Luzhkov, asking him to cancel plans to visit Sevastopol next week for an official unveiling of new housing for officers of the Black Sea Fleet.

Only President Boris Yeltsin could enforce a resolution by Russia's upper house of parliament to reclaim the port. The Russian government's official position is that it has no territorial claims on Ukraine.
But the comments -- and the arrest of a Ukrainian ship by Russian border guards patrolling Georgian territorial waters this month -- have sparked harsh criticism from Kiev.
"I will not evaluate the actions of those who have gone as far as making territorial claims on Ukraine in detail. The danger of their position is obvious," Kuchma said.
But he added: "Threats -- even going as far as promising to use force -- are not the best way of running international affairs in general and especially not with states like Ukraine".

Neighboring Russia and Ukraine have been bickering over the former Soviet fleet since Kiev won independence five years ago. Recently the dispute has centred on how to divide up the fleet's shore bases in and around Sevastopol.
Yeltsin has cancelled six trips to Ukraine to sign a Friendship Treaty because the issue has not been resolved.

However Kuchma was not entirely gloomy about the future, saying: "We are expecting, at long last, that a visit by the Russian president will take place," referring to a promise by Yeltsin to make Kiev his first post-surgery port of call.

"Actions always lead to reactions and the situation must not be brought to the boiling point. Irresponsible speeches by famous figures in Russia arouse a corresponding reaction from our hotheads as well," Kuchma added.

Kuchma said he hoped "good will, political wisdom and simple common sense will gain the upper hand in this issue at long last" but warned: "The main thing is that we do not achieve the desired result too late and at too high a price."
Crimea was transferred to Ukraine from Russia in 1954. Many of its inhabitants feel little loyalty to Kiev and look to Moscow for protection.
